text.text: Methodological flexibility-researcher degrees of freedom in procedure and scoringcan contribute to poor measurement and low replicability of findings.

To quantify methodological flexibility in the Iowa Gambling Task (IGT), a widely used measure of decision-making in clinical psychology, we conducted a meta-method review of a random sample of 100 studies.
We found prevalent underreporting and wide-spread modifications of procedural details.
We identified 244 distinct scores used to quantify IGT outcomes, 177 of which appeared only once in our sample.
To quantify the potential impact of this flexibility, we performed a multiverse analysis using 196 eligible scores on an open IGT dataset.
Correlations among these ranged from rs = -0.942 to 0.998 with a median r = 0.022, suggesting that different scoring strategies can produce extremely different study outcomes.
Given these findings, without substantive information about which specific procedural and scoring choices were employed, results from the IGT are rendered uninterpretable.
Given its wide applications, the IGT is considered to be one of the most frequently used measures for decision-making used by researchers as well as clinicians (Buelow & Barnhart, 2018a).
text.formatted: Given its wide applications, the IGT is considered to be one of the most frequently used measures for decision-making used by researchers as well as clinicians <ref type="bibr">(Buelow & Barnhart, 2018a)</ref>.

text.text: In the original IGT paradigm (Bechara et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?C2II1t 1994) https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?mz7Cvh later also referred to as the ABCD variant (Bechara et al., 2000) , in each of 100 trials subjects select one out of four decks (A, B, C, D) and draw a card.
text.formatted: In the original IGT paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bechara et al., 1994)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?C2II1t">,</ref> later also referred to as the ABCD variant <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bechara et al., 2000)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?mz7Cvh">,</ref> in each of 100 trials subjects select one out of four decks (A, B, C, D) and draw a card.

text.text: All cards provide a reward, which is the same within each deck but varies between decks: $100 for decks A and B, and $50 for decks C and D. In addition, some cards incur penalties of variable amounts, and they are unevenly distributed across decks: A and C have smaller, more frequent penalties (50% of cards), while decks B and D have larger, infrequent penalties (10% of cards).
Decks A and B are disadvantageous, with penalties in the long run outweighing the higher initial rewards.
Conversely, decks C and D are advantageous in the long term, offering smaller but more consistent rewards exceeding penalties over intervals of 10 cards.

Thus, the optimal strategy involves selecting predominantly from the advantageous decks C and D. In the original variant, which used physical cards and money, the sequence of rewards and penalties within each deck was predefined, whereas modern, computerized variants usually randomize them.
Participants start with a loan of $2000 and are instructed to maximize their net wins, though they are initially unaware of the underlying reward and penalty structure.

The initially proposed scoring methods were (1) card counts by deck across the entire task, and (2) subtracting the number of selections from the disadvantageous decks (A+B) from those of the advantageous decks (C+D) as a measure of overall task performance, the so-called net score.
The task was originally developed as a neuropsychological measure to detect decision-making impairments in patients with ventromedial prefrontal brain damage .
Patients in the original study were shown to be motivated by immediate prospects and neglecting long-term consequences, resulting in adverse decisions in the IGT as in real life.

The study used a three-group design: 44 healthy controls (21 women, 23 men; age range 20-79 years; roughly equal proportions with high school and college education) recruited without a documented procedure; a brain-damaged control group of nine participants (3 women, 6 men; age range 20-71 years) with occipital, temporal, or dorsolateral frontal lesions; and a target group of six patients (4 men, 2 women; age range 43-84 years) with ventromedial prefrontal lesions.
text.formatted: The study used a three-group design: 44 healthy controls (21 women, 23 men; age range 20-79 years; roughly equal proportions with high school and college education) recruited without a documented procedure; a brain-damaged control group of nine participants <ref type="bibr">(3 women, 6</ref> men; age range 20-71 years) with occipital, temporal, or dorsolateral frontal lesions; and a target group of six patients (4 men, 2 women; age range 43-84 years) with ventromedial prefrontal lesions.

text.text: Both clinical groups were drawn from a clinical registry on the basis of documented decision-making impairment.
No psychometric properties were reported.
Notably, one should not think of the "Iowa Gambling Task" as a unique, well-defined paradigm; rather, it has evolved into a franchise with multiple paradigms co-existing under the same name.
The degree of standardization of these paradigms can be conceptualized as a continuum.
Study-specific adhoc modifications of the IGT represent one extreme of this continuum.
They may be untested, insufficiently documented, and are unlikely to be used in multiple studies.
They may be implemented by researchers to address the specific circumstances of a single study, or to answer a question that current IGT variants are not ideally designed to answer.
Such modifications may cover a range of adjustments, such as providing additional instructions or modifying the visual presentation.
However, without comprehensive documentation of such modifications, the exact procedure may not easily be recreated.

On the other end of the continuum, there are established adaptations of the IGT, characterized by distinct, predefined design choices and rules and typically accompanied by published protocols, and clearly defined, reproducible procedures.
However, varying degrees of standardization can be observed between these two extremes, thereby making a categorial distinction impracticable.
In the following, we will refer to different versions and adaptations of the IGT as variants, regardless of their degree of standardization.
Although the IGT was created in 1994, an IGT variant accompanied by a manual and norm data was not published until 2007 (Bechara, 2007 (Bechara, , 2016)).
text.formatted: Although the IGT was created in 1994, an IGT variant accompanied by a manual and norm data was not published until 2007 <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bechara, 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bechara, , 2016))</ref>.

text.text: During this interval, the same authors developed several variants of the original IGT (Bechara et al., 1999 (Bechara et al., , 2000)).
text.formatted: During this interval, the same authors developed several variants of the original IGT <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bechara et al., 1999</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bechara et al., , 2000))</ref>.

text.text: Other researchers have sought to align the IGT with specific requirements of diverse research questionshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?sRId3Z study designs (e.g., for use in an fMRI, Tanabe et al., 2007) , and sample characteristics (e.g., adolescents, Overman et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Other researchers have sought to align the IGT with specific requirements of diverse research questions, study designs (e.g., for use in an fMRI, <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Tanabe et al., 2007)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?sRId3Z">,</ref> and sample characteristics (e.g., adolescents, <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Overman et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: These developments reflect the growing heterogeneity of the IGT paradigm.
A first computerized variant (Bechara et al., 1999) introduced visual feedback and more detailed instructions to the participants, including a recommendation to avoid disadvantageous decks.
text.formatted: A first computerized variant <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bechara et al., 1999)</ref> introduced visual feedback and more detailed instructions to the participants, including a recommendation to avoid disadvantageous decks.

text.text: This variant divided the 100 trials into five blocks à 20 trials, enabling the calculation of a learning index from net scores (see Box 1) for each block separately.

Further variants introduced by the same authors (Bechara et al., 2000) include the A'B'C'D' variant, in which increasing penalties in the disadvantageous decks (A', B') and decreasing penalties in the advantageous decks (C', D') widen the deck contrasts over time; the EFGH variant, an inverse of the ABCD variant, featuring immediate penalties and intermittent rewards; and the E'F'G'H' variant, an inverse of the A'B'C'D' variant, in which the reward schedules shift analogously across blocks.
text.formatted: Further variants introduced by the same authors <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bechara et al., 2000)</ref> include the A'B'C'D' variant, in which increasing penalties in the disadvantageous decks (A', B') and decreasing penalties in the advantageous decks (C', D') widen the deck contrasts over time; the EFGH variant, an inverse of the ABCD variant, featuring immediate penalties and intermittent rewards; and the E'F'G'H' variant, an inverse of the A'B'C'D' variant, in which the reward schedules shift analogously across blocks.

text.text: While the original IGT was primarily developed for clinical research, the clinical IGT (Bechara, 2007 (Bechara, , 2016) ) was specifically designed for diagnostic purposes.
text.formatted: While the original IGT was primarily developed for clinical research, the clinical IGT <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bechara, 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bechara, , 2016) )</ref> was specifically designed for diagnostic purposes.

text.text: It is accompanied by a manual for standardized administration, norm data, and instructions for interpretation of results, and resembles the A'B'C'D' variant but instead of fixed rewards it uses variable amounts that average to $100 (decks A and B) and $50 (decks C and D).
text.formatted: It is accompanied by a manual for standardized administration, norm data, and instructions for interpretation of results, and resembles the A'B'C'D' variant but instead of fixed rewards it uses variable amounts that average to $100 <ref type="bibr">(decks A and B)</ref> and $50 (decks C and D).

text.text: The software allows the adjustment of various procedural parameters, including intertrial interval duration, number of trials, and loan.
It calculates primary raw scores, total net score, block net scores, total money won, and reaction times.
Furthermore, the clinical variant incorporates conversions of raw scores to T-scores and percentile ranks for different age groups and educational levels.

The normative sample comprised 932 adults (45.3% male; M age = 48.58, SD = 21.66, range = 18-95; M education = 14.99 years, SD = 2.69) aggregated from multiple sites, with a U.S. Census-matched subsample of 264 adults (49.2% male; M age = 45.23, SD = 19.42, range 18-90) available for comparison.

The 2016 revision (IGT2) extended the norms to children and adolescents aged 8 to 17 years, based on an additional U.S. Census-matched sample of 453 participants (51% male; M age = 12.43, SD = 2.89) (Bechara, 2016).
text.formatted: The 2016 revision (IGT2) extended the norms to children and adolescents aged 8 to 17 years, based on an additional U.S. Census-matched sample of 453 participants (51% male; M age = 12.43, SD = 2.89) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bechara, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Despite being a commercially distributed clinical instrument, the manual contains no test-retest reliability data, internal consistency estimates, or standard errors.
This gap was identified as a central limitation shortly after its publication (Buelow & Suhr, 2009) and remained unaddressed in subsequent editions.
text.formatted: This gap was identified as a central limitation shortly after its publication <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Buelow & Suhr, 2009)</ref> and remained unaddressed in subsequent editions.

All monetary values are presented in US-Dollars ($) as reported in the original sources.

Although some of these procedural differences may appear technical or minor, there is evidence that they affect performance metrics, i.e. the scores thought to reflect (dis)advantageous decisionmaking.

For examplehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?YFPZ6g additional trials were shown to improve IGT performance (Overman & Pierce, 2013) , as do more comprehensive instructions, particularly when participants are advised to avoid specific decks (Balodis et al., 2006; Fernie & Tunney, 2006).

text.text: A better performance in trials 21 to 60 in the clinical IGT, compared to the original IGT, suggests differences in the learning curves between these variants (Buelow & Barnhart, 2018a).
text.formatted: A better performance in trials 21 to 60 in the clinical IGT, compared to the original IGT, suggests differences in the learning curves between these variants <ref type="bibr">(Buelow & Barnhart, 2018a)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, a variety of scoring methods have been explored, complicating the comparability of studies (Barnhart & Buelow, 2021).
text.formatted: Furthermore, a variety of scoring methods have been explored, complicating the comparability of studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barnhart & Buelow, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For examplehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?YFX7Lk in addition to the net score and card counts by deck (see Box 1), overall performance has been measured by monetary outcome (Shurman et al., 2005) , or by choices from decks A and D only (D-A) (Gansler et al., 2011).
text.formatted: For example, in addition to the net score and card counts by deck (see Box 1), overall performance has been measured by monetary outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Shurman et al., 2005)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?YFX7Lk">,</ref> or by choices from decks A and D only (D-A) <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Gansler et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Another approach has been to evaluate overall performance based on loss-frequency as reflected by the metric [(B+D)-(A+C)] rather than long-term outcome-based scoring as reflected by the typically used net score [(C+D)-(A+B)] in order to reduce false positives on impairment (Barnhart & Buelow, 2021).
text.formatted: Another approach has been to evaluate overall performance based on loss-frequency as reflected by the metric [(B+D)-(A+C)] rather than long-term outcome-based scoring as reflected by the typically used net score [(C+D)-(A+B)] in order to reduce false positives on impairment <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barnhart & Buelow, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Learning curves have been calculated using three (Case & Olino, 2020) or four blocks (Bark et al., 2005) instead of five.
text.formatted: Learning curves have been calculated using three <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Case & Olino, 2020)</ref> or four blocks <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bark et al., 2005)</ref> instead of five.

text.text: Different scoring methods have also been linked to distinct constructs.

For example, earlier trials are postulated to reflect decision-making under ambiguity, whereas the later trials are thought to reflect decisionmaking under risk (Brand et al., 2007; Noël et al., 2007).
text.formatted: For example, earlier trials are postulated to reflect decision-making under ambiguity, whereas the later trials are thought to reflect decisionmaking under risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Brand et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Noël et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Behavior throughout the task has also been examined, for example, by the number of deck switches (Smart & Krawitz, 2015).
text.formatted: Behavior throughout the task has also been examined, for example, by the number of deck switches <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Smart & Krawitz, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the IGT's widespread use, these differences in procedures and scoring methods are underappreciated in the IGT literature.
Different variants are often treated as interchangeable (Buelow & Barnhart, 2018a).
text.formatted: Different variants are often treated as interchangeable <ref type="bibr">(Buelow & Barnhart, 2018a)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers may underreport or fail to specify which variant they used, or how they modified the IGT, further obscuring the evidence base.

Although a task's modification may be justifiable, it can limit the comparability of results, raise concerns over the robustness of research findings (e.g. when certain findings only occur under very specific task modifications, but claims are generalised to "the IGT"), and lead to inconsistent or misleading conclusions (Elson et al., 2023; Flake & Fried, 2020).
text.formatted: Although a task's modification may be justifiable, it can limit the comparability of results, raise concerns over the robustness of research findings (e.g. when certain findings only occur under very specific task modifications, but claims are generalised to "the IGT"), and lead to inconsistent or misleading conclusions <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Elson et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Flake & Fried, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Variability in methodological procedures and scoring methods pose a particular problem for research synthesis, as studies nominally using the same method might actually measure different constructs (a validity problem), and excluding any study deviating from a standard protocol limits the evidence base that can be considered (an efficiency problem) as well as introducing selection bias.
To understand how the IGT literature deals with methodological flexibility, we examined metaanalyses of IGT studies.
We conducted a Scopus search on April 23, 2024 for "Iowa gambling task" AND "meta-analysis" in title, abstract, keywords.
The results were then ranked by citations.
After initially selecting the 15 most cited meta-analyses, we excluded one that did not include the IGT, and added the 16th ranked meta-analysis to maintain a final set of 15.
We examined these 15 meta-analyses (M1 to M15, see Table S1 in the Supplementary Material) for any indication that variability was accounted for, e.g. in the inclusion/exclusion of IGT studies.
text.formatted: We examined these 15 meta-analyses (M1 to M15, see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref> in the Supplementary Material) for any indication that variability was accounted for, e.g. in the inclusion/exclusion of IGT studies.

text.text: We updated our search on January 8, 2026, which yielded the same set of 15 meta-analyses.
Procedural aspects of the IGT played essentially no role in the eligibility criteria of the examined meta-analyses.
M9 explicitly states that they did not exclude studies based on procedure.
Only M8 and M12 excluded modified IGT versions but never defined what constitutes a modification or which IGT variant(s) they considered non-modified.
Overall, this illustrates the limited consideration given to variability in IGT procedures across studies.
In contrast, the meta-analyses gave more consideration to consistency in scoring methods.
Six meta-analyses restricted the scoring methods to the net score [(C+D)-(A+B)] (M1, M2, M4, M6, M8, M10) while three meta-analyses (M11, M12, M15) additionally included block scores.
These metaanalyses reported different strategies for handling studies without available net scores.
Seven metaanalyses (M1, M2, M4, M8, M10, M11, M15) obtained additional data from study authors.

Five of them (M1, M2, M4, M8, M11) excluded studies when no additional data could be obtained, either because authors did not respond or the required information was missing, while two (M10, M15) did not specify how they handled cases where no net scores could be obtained.
In two meta-analyses (M8, M12), missing values were extracted from figures where possible.
Finally, one meta-analysis (M6) did not provide any information on how missing net scores were handled.
M3 and M9 reported using a "total score" for all included studies, but did not sufficiently describe this score (i.e. it is unclear if this was also the net score, or something else).
M14 included studies with a range of different scoring methods, among them block scores for all blocks, the last three blocks, the mean, the net score, and overall monetary gain.
Three meta-analyses (M5, M7, M13) did not specify any scoring method, and we have to assume potential differences between included studies were not accounted for.

In summary, while the majority of meta-analyses address heterogeneity in scoring methods to some extent, they do not do so consistently, and often relevant information is missing to fully appreciate the methodology.

Taking the heterogeneity of procedures and scoring methods into consideration is not standard practice when conducting meta-analyses with the IGT, and there is no obvious way to control for the heterogeneity because its effects are poorly understood.
Consequently, there are inherent issues with the comparability of the studies that are aggregated in meta-analyses.

However, in the absence of a systematic assessment of this methodological heterogeneity in the IGT literature, meta-analysts may not feel it's necessary to address it in their inclusion criteria or statistical analyses.

The objective of meta-method reviews (Elson, 2019) is to understand the extent of methodological flexibility that exists within a given research area, and to complement research synthesis with a systematic review of research practices that produces the effect sizes included in meta-analyses.
text.formatted: The objective of meta-method reviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Elson, 2019)</ref> is to understand the extent of methodological flexibility that exists within a given research area, and to complement research synthesis with a systematic review of research practices that produces the effect sizes included in meta-analyses.

text.text: The issue of methodological flexibility has particular relevance to IGT research where despite the introduction of a clinical variant with the intent to standardize the task, there remains a lack of consensus on a unified standard, resulting in persistent variability of procedures and scoring methods.
To summarize, the IGT comprises multiple variants with a varying degree of standardization, which we are referring to as methodological flexibility.
This methodological flexibility may pose a significant threat to the task's validity and its replicability in clinical research.
Our meta-method analysis aims to estimate the prevalence and impact of this flexibility across the literature.
Specifically, we seek to answer the following research questions: 1.
Which variations in the procedures of the IGT are reported in published psychological research?
Which variations in the scoring methods of the IGT are reported in published psychological research?
How frequently are variations in the procedures and scoring methods of the IGT reported in psychological research?
How transparently are the procedures and scoring methods of the IGT reported?
How often is relevant information missing?
How do the identified variations in scoring methods of the IGT affect the robustness of IGT outcomes?
The systematic review and an earlier version of the codebook were preregistered (https://osf.io/ywhda).
text.formatted: The systematic review and an earlier version of the codebook were preregistered (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/ywhda">https://osf.io/ywhda</ref>).

text.text: The multiverse analysis was not preregistered.
The codebooks used to classify procedural features and scoring strategies required iterative changes to accommodate what we observed in the literature.

The changes are documented in a folder ('method_development') on the GitHub repository (see below), including the old codebook, the original approach to capturing scoring strategies, a set of examples illustrating pitfalls of this approach, and data of two pilot test runs of the final codebooks.
The final codebooks can be found in the 'method' folder, along with instructions on how to use them.
All data, materials, and code are available in a public Github repository (https://github.com/anniria/igt-methodological-flexibility).
text.formatted: All data, materials, and code are available in a public Github repository (<ref type="url" target="https://github.com/anniria/igt-methodological-flexibility">https://github.com/anniria/igt-methodological- flexibility</ref>).

text.text: As this is a systematic review, this study involved an analysis of existing data rather than new data collection.
In line with the journal's reporting standards for such work, we have provided a full description of the analyses conducted.
This includes the procedure for our systematic database search, the criteria for population definition and sampling, the rules for study inclusion and exclusion, and the method for data extraction.
Ethical approval was not required for this study as it involved a systematic review and analysis of previously published literature.
The sampling procedure followed several steps.
First, we conducted a systematic database search with few limiters to define the population of IGT literature.
From the population, we randomly drew publications.
If they were eligible based on our predefined inclusion criteria, we added them to the final sample.
Sampling was stopped when the final sample included N = 100 publications.
We defined the population with a systematic search of the databases APA PsycInfo and APA PsycArticles using the database provider EBSCOhost.

The database search was conducted as a full text search with the search string "Iowa Gambling Task OR Bechara's Gambling Task" and the following limiters: Publication type: academic (peer-reviewed) journal; Language: English OR German; Methodology: empirical study; Population group: human; Age: adulthood (18 years and older).
Database search and retrieval of records were performed on May 2 nd , 2022 and resulted in 1510 hits.
After automatic removal of exact duplicates by EBSCOhost, 1487 results remained.

We exported the population list to an Excel file and randomly rearranged the rows in R (version 4.2.0; https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?LpJ31L) using the package openxlsx (version 4.2.4; Schauberger & Walker, 2022).
text.formatted: We exported the population list to an Excel file and randomly rearranged the rows in R (version 4.2.0; <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?LpJ31L">R Core Team, 2023</ref>) using the package openxlsx (version 4.2.4; <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Schauberger & Walker, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Working our way down from the top row, articles were assessed against the following inclusion criteria: (1) primary data were collected, (2) the IGT was administered and scored in at least one reported study.
We excluded articles that we were not able to access the full text of.
Publications that were eligible were added to the sample iteratively.
In total, we examined 140 articles until 100 met the inclusion criteria.
One article was excluded because we did not have access to the full text, and one because it was part of our training sample (see below).
We stopped the sampling procedure at N = 100 publications in the final sample.
For articles reporting multiple IGT studies, we only considered the last study.
We developed two codebooks, separating the coding of IGT procedures from scoring methods.
During development, the codebooks were tested on 15 IGT publications that were not included in the final sample.
Along with the codebooks, we developed instructions on how to complete the codebooks, as well as a set of examples to clarify the coding rules.
Two trained raters independently extracted procedural and scoring details for each study.
When multiple IGT variants were used in a single study (N = 6 studies) all variants were coded.

When a target article cited another publication for information about the procedure, the details in the cited publication, if accessible, were used to complete the coding for the target article (N = 21 studies).
In cases where information was missing, ambiguous, or vague, or when we were unable to access a publication referred to for more details, this was recorded as indeterminable.
General ambiguities or questions regarding the procedure or scoring methods were recorded in an additional column.

The procedure codebook captured information on (a) which IGT variant was used, (b) number of trials administered, (c) goal of the task (i.e., the task objective communicated to the participants), (d) the feedback subjects received throughout the task, (e) incentives for participating in the study (e.g., in some cases the subjects' compensation for participation depended on their task performance), (f) as well as the starting loan, and (g) the currency used.
Several variables also captured (h) the task's gain/loss schedule.
Here, we collected several task parameters frequently reported when describing the IGT.

These included the rewards for advantageous and disadvantageous decks, the probabilities of penalties for each deck, and the amount of net gains or losses over a fixed interval of card selections from each deck along with that interval.
These values are essential for accurately replicating a specific application of the IGT.

With regard to identifying the specific IGT procedure employed within a given study, we found that merely relying on citations of an IGT publication or variant was not appropriate, for example, because authors often cite several conflicting sources or it is not clear whether they are merely making a general reference to the original IGT.
Therefore, we only accepted references that the authors explicitly linked to their specific task procedure.
Additionally, we sought to confirm that the information provided regarding the implementation of the IGT was consistent with the procedure referenced.

Regarding the instructions and goals of the task communicated to the subjects, as well as the feedback that the subjects received during the task, we determined whether these were equivalent to or deviated from the original task.

As reference we used the paper introducing the first computerized version (Bechara et al. 1999) https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?U4eD0R which the authors describe as based on the original 1994 task and provides the most detailed account of the instructions and feedback given to participants.
text.formatted: As reference we used the paper introducing the first computerized version <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bechara et al. 1999)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?U4eD0R">,</ref> which the authors describe as based on the original 1994 task and provides the most detailed account of the instructions and feedback given to participants.

text.text: Any identifiable departure that altered the conceptual content of the instructions or feedback, e.g. providing additional strategic hints or changing the outcome information displayed, was coded as a deviation.
Surface-level differences, such as a minor change in wording, were not.
We defined a score as a separate numerical value that is generated from IGT data and used in data analysis.
We only included IGT scores that were explicitly mentioned being calculated or derived, and did not include scores that were either logically or implicitly calculated.

For instance, whenever a paper reported using the net score [(C+D)-(A+B)], this was coded as a single score, despite the fact that to calculate the net score, the individual deck choices have to be calculated first, each of which represents a distinct scoring method that researchers could use to analyze IGT data (and perhaps do, in other papers).

Similarly, when an analysis was based on a difference score between two net scores (e.g., net score on the first half of trials minus net score on the second half of trials), we coded the difference as a single score if the two net scores were not used separately in any analyses.
However, when multiple scores were computed for a joint analysis, these were coded as separate scores.
For example, a learning curve analysis based on 5 blocks of 20 trials was coded as 5 separate scores.
In case the details of a scoring method could not be determined or understood from its description, the score was coded as indeterminable.

All indeterminable scores were classified as unique scoring methods, given that it was not possible to ascertain whether they were equivalent to each other or a specific determinable score reported elsewhere.
Scores were coded individually for each study and each distinct score was assigned a unique score ID.
This meant that a score ID could be represented multiple times in the dataset if the same score was used in multiple studies.
Scores that were numerically different but perfectly correlated were grouped before analysis to prevent an overestimation of distinct scoring methods.

For example, selections from advantageous decks [C+D] or disadvantageous decks [A+B] are deterministic linear transformations of the net score [(C+D)-(A+B)] and were therefore collapsed into a single scoring method.
text.formatted: For example, selections from advantageous decks <ref type="bibr">[C+D]</ref> or disadvantageous decks [A+B] are deterministic linear transformations of the net score [(C+D)-(A+B)] and were therefore collapsed into a single scoring method.

text.text: The full materials, including worked examples, may be useful to researchers conducting metamethods analyses of other tasks (see the Transparency and Openness section).
We computed the interrater reliability for all variables in the procedure codebook, yielding a mean Cohen's κ = .70 (SD = .10), with a range from .44 to .90.
According to the criteria of Landis & Koch, (1977) a κ of .70 indicates that, overall, there was substantial agreement between the raters.
text.formatted: According to the criteria of <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Landis & Koch, (1977)</ref> a κ of .70 indicates that, overall, there was substantial agreement between the raters.

text.text: The range suggests that there was only moderate agreement for some variables (e.g., whether there were deviations in the instructions of a given task, κ = .44, bootstrap SE = .09, 95% CI [.26, .61]) and very high agreement for others (e.g., how many trials were performed in a given task, κ = .90, bootstrap SE = .06, 95% CI [.76, 1.00]).
We provide a detailed account in Table S2 in the Supplementary Material.
text.formatted: We provide a detailed account in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref> in the Supplementary Material.

text.text: There were three main reasons for disagreements: (1) Human error (by the coders); (2) Ambiguous task descriptions; (3) Conflicting task descriptions.
Examples for (2) and ( 3) are provided in the Underreporting section.
text.formatted: Examples for (2) and ( <ref type="formula">3</ref>) are provided in the Underreporting section.

text.text: To assess inter-rater reliability for the scoring codebook, we used a multi-metric approach.
Cohen's κ is based on the assumption that all raters classify the same fixed set of items into mutually exclusive categories.
This assumption does not apply to our data set, as raters were required to assign multiple scores per article, and the total number and types of scores could vary between raters and articles.
Consequently, it was not feasible to simply calculate Cohen's κ for the entire data set.

Instead, we decided to use three informative indicators of reliability: 1) We calculated Krippendorff's α for ratio-scaled data to assess the interrater reliability of the score count per article (α = .90, bootstrap SE = .02, 95% CI [.85, .94]).
2) We examined whether the two raters identified the same scores within each article.

For each article, the raters' score lists were aligned into pairs: score IDs identified by both raters were paired with each other, IDs identified by only one rater were paired with the other rater's unmatched IDs or, if none remained, with an explicit "no score" category.
Unweighted Cohen's κ was then computed across all pairs, with score IDs and "no score" as nominal categories (κ = .80, bootstrap SE = .01, 95% CI [.77, .83]).
Because IDs identified by only one rater cannot match by construction, κ is invariant to how these are paired.

3) We compared how frequently each score was used across the entire sample by calculating Krippendorff's α for ratio-scaled data for the occurrence of each score in the entire sample (α = .92, bootstrap SE = .02, 95% CI [.87, .95]).
Overall, these values indicate a high level of agreement between raters.
All disagreements between the two raters were inspected and resolved through discussion and mutual agreement.
The agreed upon codes were then integrated into a set of master codebooks that were used in the data analysis.

text.text: As preregistered, the final sample after applying inclusion/exclusion criteria included 100 articles drawn randomly from a defined population of articles.
Years of publication ranged from 2002 to 2021.

Coincidentally, we classified exactly 50 studies as clinical based on their research topic, such as substance use, gambling, ADHD, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, eating disorders, Parkinson's disease, and autism.

The remaining 50 studies were categorized as non-clinical, and covered a wide range of topics, such as age differences in decisionmaking processes, emotion regulation, impulsivity, driving behavior, sleep deprivation, and others.
Sample sizes across all studies ranged from 10 to 5227 subjects with a median of 65 (see Table 2).
text.formatted: Sample sizes across all studies ranged from 10 to 5227 subjects with a median of 65 (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Of the 100 articles, six included two variants of the IGT, resulting in 106 coded IGT procedures.
In the following, we present the descriptive results per IGT rather than per article.
A core finding was the prevalence of vague, ambiguous, and incomplete reporting of the majority of procedural details that we collected.

This phenomenon was especially prominent in clinical studies with an overall rate of 65.63% indeterminable procedural details compared to 45.04% in non-clinical studies (see Fig. 1 as well as Table S3 in the Supplementary Material for a detailed account per variable).
text.formatted: This phenomenon was especially prominent in clinical studies with an overall rate of 65.63% indeterminable procedural details compared to 45.04% in non-clinical studies (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> as well as Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref> in the Supplementary Material for a detailed account per variable).

text.text: While the clinical IGT (Bechara, 2007 (Bechara, , 2016) ) comes with standardized documentation that might make additional reporting seem unnecessary, only one clinical study in our sample actually used it.
text.formatted: While the clinical IGT <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bechara, 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bechara, , 2016) )</ref> comes with standardized documentation that might make additional reporting seem unnecessary, only one clinical study in our sample actually used it.

text.text: The high rate of indeterminable procedural details in clinical studies therefore cannot be attributed to its use.

Although we tried to complete missing information whenever a paper made a clear reference to another study for the task's procedural details, these details often remained partially or completely indeterminable.

In the majority of cases it was not possible to identify the specifics of the instructions, goal, and feedback provided, as well as whether any modifications had been made to them: In 42 cases (39.60%), information on goal, instructions, and feedback was incomplete, and in 27 cases (25.50%) entirely absent.
For example, an article would specify that the subjects were instructed to maximize their wins, but it would not indicate whether other instructions were provided.
Similarly, in 15 cases (14.20%), the descriptions of the gainloss schedules were incomplete, meaning that possible deviations could not be identified.
In further 58 cases (54.70%), information on the gainloss schedules was missing completely.

While in these cases no deviations could be identified from the descriptions provided, the descriptions themselves were also insufficient to conclude that the original IGT's gain-loss schedule was adhered to.
Note.
The figure displays the percentage of IGTs in clinical (N = 53) and non-clinical (N = 53) studies for which specific IGT parameters were indeterminable, split into.
For clarity, several related parameters were collapsed by averaging their percentages.

Specifically, Reward per Card averages the values for advantageous and disadvantageous decks; Gain/Loss per 10 Cards averages the four variables for net gains and losses across decks; Gain/Loss Interval averages the four variables for the card interval over which the net gains and losses are defined; and Loss Frequency averages the four variables for loss frequency across all decks.
(See Table S3 in the Supplementary Material for a detailed account per variable.)
text.formatted: (See Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref> in the Supplementary Material for a detailed account per variable.)

text.text: IGT = Iowa Gambling Task.
Notably, references provided by the authors for further details on the procedure sometimes led to further inconsistencies.
To illustrate, at least two papers reference Bechara et al. (2000) for more details of the procedure employed.
text.formatted: To illustrate, at least two papers reference <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bechara et al. (2000)</ref> for more details of the procedure employed.

text.text: However, Bechara et al. (2000) themselves describe four different IGT variants.
text.formatted: However, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bechara et al. (2000)</ref> themselves describe four different IGT variants.

text.text: In another case, two publications were referenced for more details on the methods used, but each cited article used slightly different task variants.
Some target articles cite another reference for further details of its methods which, in turn, cite yet other references for the details of their methods.

In any of these examples, the ambiguity of referenced materials and a lack of further specifications in the target articles makes it difficult if not impossible to understand the details of the procedure actually used.
Across our sample, we found modifications to all procedural details we investigated.
These ranged from extensive changes, affecting the entire task, to modifications limited in scope, affecting only one or two features.

In the majority of cases (N = 62, 58.49%), it was indeterminable whether the procedure had been modified or not, whereas in 40 cases (37.74%), at least one procedural aspect clearly had been modified.
Of these, the clinical IGT (Bechara, 2007) was used in two cases (1.89%), which we classified as modification of the original IGT due to its inherently different gain-loss schedule.
text.formatted: Of these, the clinical IGT <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bechara, 2007)</ref> was used in two cases (1.89%), which we classified as modification of the original IGT due to its inherently different gain-loss schedule.

text.text: However, since this version contains adjustable settings (e.g., starting capital) that went unreported, it was not possible to determine if further modifications were made.
Only four (3.77%) IGTs matched the original IGT without any modification (Bechara et al., 1994).
text.formatted: Only four (3.77%) IGTs matched the original IGT without any modification <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bechara et al., 1994)</ref>.

text.text: In the following, we report the rates of modifications as well as the rates of missing information per task feature.
The majority of IGTs (N = 89, 83.96%) consisted of 100 trials.
In nine instances (8.49%), the number of trials differed from 100 (range: 50 to 400), and in the remaining eight instances (7.55%), the number of trials was not reported.
In some cases, the deviations from the standard 100 trials constituted an integral component of more comprehensive modifications to the overall task.
For example, one IGT consisted of 400 trials, with the contingencies reversed after 200 trials so that the advantageous decks became the disadvantageous decks and vice versa.
Another example is the adaptation for use in an MRI scanner, which involved the inclusion of additional control trials.
In these control trials, subjects were instructed to select a card, but no gain or loss was assigned to it.
The goal of win maximization was mentioned in 68 instances (64.15%), and in 37 instances (34.91%), the task goal was not reported.
A different goal was set for the participants in one task (0.94%) in which participants were specifically instructed to win $5,000, with the objective of eliciting anxiety during the task.
In 77 instances (72.64%), it was indeterminable whether participants received the original or deviating task instructions.

In 15 instances (14.15%), participants received the original instructions, and in 14 instances (13.21%), participants received modified instructions including, for example, the hint that participants can maximize their win by selecting cards from good decks, or disclosing the number of trials to be completed.
Further deviations include instructions to make a choice within a specific time limit (e.g., 2 seconds or less), or even disclosing in advance which decks were advantageous in the long run.
Most of the time (N = 74, 69.81%) it was indeterminable whether participants received the original task feedback.
Where determinable, feedback was modified more often (N = 21, 19.81%) than kept unchanged (N = 11, 10.38%).
Deviations from the original feedback included, for example, additional stimuli, such as images (e.g., brands or faces) on the reverse side of the decks.
In one study, participants not only got to observe the outcome of the selected deck but of all other decks.

Taken together, only 9 tasks (8.49%) were aligned with the original task in terms of instructions, goal, and feedback, while changes to at least one of these procedural characteristics were identified in 28 instances (26.40%).
As reported above, the descriptions of the gainloss-schedule were missing or incomplete in the majority of instances (N = 73, 68.87%).
In 17 cases (16.00%), the gain-loss schedule of the original task was adhered to.
In 16 cases (15.10%), substantial deviations were documented.
These deviations were in some cases a consequence of the employment of the clinical IGT or a reversed IGT.
In other instances, the deviations were due to setting losses to zero, modifications to the probabilities of losses for specific decks, or the use of differing win amounts per card.
Another task involved an alteration resulting in decks B and D being identical to decks A and C, thus establishing a uniform loss probability across all decks.
A total of 806 scores were identified across all 106 IGTs in the 100 sampled studies.
Of these, 244 were determined to be mathematically distinct ways of scoring IGT data (i.e., were non-redundant after excluding different labels or descriptions of the same underlying math).
The number of scores per IGT ranged from 1 to 49, with a mode of 6 (median = 6, mean = 7.58, SD = 7.42).
Note, that for this summary two scores were excluded because they were calculated across two IGTs within the same study.
Of course, if additional articles were examined, the observed number of ways the IGT is scored can only remain the same or, more likely, increase.
This raises the question of what the total population of ways IGT data is scored is in the population (i.e., the literature).
Our results in Table 3 imply at least 414 possible scoring strategies (23 columns multiplied by 18 rows) among the already observed features.
text.formatted: Our results in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> imply at least 414 possible scoring strategies (23 columns multiplied by 18 rows) among the already observed features.

text.text: It is possible that other features exist.
Another approach to estimating the total population of scores from our observed sample comes from the use of Richness Estimation, a statistical approach used in ecology.
There, it is used to answer questions such as "I have observed X number of species (sample), so how many are likely to exist in this habitat (population)?".

We applied the bias-corrected Chao2, treating each of the 100 articles as a sampling unit and each of the 244 distinct scoring methods as a species; a method used multiple times within the same article counted as a single presence.
The estimate is driven by the number of methods observed in exactly one article (Q1 = 184) and in exactly two articles (Q2 = 38).
Because Chao2 provides a lower bound on true richness, we estimate that the IGT literature includes at least 685 scoring methods (Chao2 = 685, SE = 98.93, 95% CI [530, 925]).
text.formatted: Because Chao2 provides a lower bound on true richness, we estimate that the IGT literature includes at least 685 scoring methods (Chao2 = 685, SE = 98.93, 95% CI <ref type="bibr">[530,</ref> <ref type="bibr">925]</ref>).

text.text: While this raises questions about meaningful differences between different scores, it serves to illustrate the point that the literature likely has many more ways to score IGT data than those already observed in our sample.

We organized the majority of distinct scores (N = 205) according to the task parameters from which they were derived (i.e. deck selections, deck switches, money won or lost, trial-to-trial learning), and the trial subsets included in the scoring (see Table 3).

text.text: Most of these scores were later included in our multiverse analysis (see below).

Scores derived from deck selections were most prevalent and included selections from all decks (e.g., the net score [(C+D)-(A+B)]), multiple decks (e.g., only choices from low loss probability decks (B+D)), or a single deck.
Additional transformations included, for example, the conversion into T-scores, dichotomizing scores using cut-offs, or a median split to distinguish impaired from unimpaired performance.

Scores were analyzed across all trials, a subset of trials (e.g., the last 40%), or as a difference score calculated by subtracting the value of one subset of trials from another (e.g., the last 60% minus the first 40%).
Deck switching scores included switches or non-switches in total or under certain conditions (e.g., the number of deck switches after a loss on deck A).
Scores related to money won or lost included net as well as total or wins or losses across the whole task.

Of the N = 39 distinct scores not included in Table 3, two were difference scores calculated across two IGT variants within the same study, and 16 were parameters from three different cognitive modelling approaches based on trial-by-trial data, i.e. the Expectancy-Valence model (Busemeyer & Stout, 2002) with three parameters, the Value-Plus-Perseveration model (Worthy et al., 2013) with eight parameters, and a proposed Temporal Difference Reinforcement Learning model with five parameters.

text.text: The remaining 21 scores could not be classified due to poor score descriptions (e.g., undefined 'improvement score') or missing task descriptions (e.g., indeterminable subsets of trials).
The modal scoring strategy in our sample was the net score [(C+D)-(A+B)] across all trials (N = 88, 10.92% of scores) used for 75 IGTs (70.75%).

Note that the discrepancy of 88 net scores in 75 tasks arises because scores such as (A+B) and (C+D), which were reported separately for some tasks, were grouped together in our analysis (see the Extraction of Scoring Details section) and were therefore counted repeatedly per task in these cases.

Another common score was the IGT learning index, consisting of net scores [(C+D)-(A+B)] for each of 5 blocks à 20 trials, and deck selections from single decks A, B, C, and D across all trials, which were often, but not always, reported in conjunction.
Together, these ten scores made up 56.82% of all scores across the sample.
For 92 IGTs (86.79%), at least one of them was reported.
Note that this table does not include scoring strategies that were not described in sufficient detail to classify (N = 21), or more complex and difficult to fit into this matrix (N = 18).
Unique Scores On the other hand, 177 distinct scores were observed only once within the sample.
These unique scores amounted to 21.96% of all scores.
For 45 IGTs at least one unique score was reported, and for 9 IGTs exclusively unique scores were reported.

To illustrate, one scoring method included splitting the 100 trials into four unequal blocks of 10, 40, 30 and 20 trials, the net scores [(C+D)-(A+B)] for the subsets of trials 11-50 and 51-80 being unique scores.
Another example was a difference score between deck selections [(C+D)-(A+B)] for block 3 and block 1, within 3 blocks of trials.
Another unusual score was the modal deck choice, which yields categorical rather than continuous values.
One score was indeterminable because it involved correlating the (categorial) deck choices, although there is no obvious way to rank them.

In other words, a significance test was performed individually for each participant.
The review demonstrated that IGT data are scored in many different ways.
In principle, this measurement flexibility can enable poor measurement, jingle fallacy, or overconditioning on results (i.e., p-hacking).
If all scoring strategies were very highly correlated with one another, this would represent a very limited problem.
At the same time, we think the observed heterogeneity in scoring would be unlikely to occur if all scores produced very similar results.

In order to understand the likely impact of this observed flexibility, we employed a multiverse analysis approach (Steegen et al., 2016) to estimate the correlations among the scoring strategies we observed in the review.

To assess whether the 196 scoring strategies can be reduced to a smaller set of interpretable dimensions, which perhaps reflect different substantive questions answerable by the IGT, we conducted a hierarchical clustering analysis to group scoring strategies based on their correlations.
Average-linkage clustering on 1r over the full set with a data-driven dynamic cut yielded 20 clusters.

Within-cluster mean correlations ranged from r = 0.42 to r = 0.86, between-cluster mean correlations reached r = 0.64, indicating that cluster boundaries mark gradients in a continuously structured metric space rather than discrete partitions (see Table S4 and Figures S1 and S2 in the Supplementary Material).

To illustrate how this translates into concrete study outcomes, we reanalysed a dataset from one of the studies in our review. Hayes & Wedell (2020b) examined whether skin conductance responses (SCRs) to choice feedback predict IGT performance in a non-clinical sample (N = 64).

Our review reveals a large heterogeneity in procedures and, in particular, scoring methods in the IGT literature, many of which are only used in a single instance.

We then show that the correlations between these scoring methods span nearly the full range from strongly negative to strongly positive, demonstrating that they should not be treated as interchangeable or even equivalent, and that the specific choice of an IGT scoring method can have dramatic effects on the outcome of a study.
Vague, ambiguous, and incomplete reporting was a core issue identified by the review.
Frequently, manuscripts report some general information, while failing to specify the necessary details to reproduce the IGT in question.
Accordingly, the actual prevalence of IGT studies matching the original protocol is unknowable.
This high rate of indeterminability limits the reproducibility of IGT studies and may threaten validity of results (Flake & Fried, 2020).
text.formatted: This high rate of indeterminability limits the reproducibility of IGT studies and may threaten validity of results <ref type="bibr">(Flake & Fried, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of precise and comprehensive descriptions of the methods makes it unfeasible for other researchers to reproduce studies or accurately interpret their findings and can result in inconsistencies in the comparison of studies, which is a severe issue for meta-analyses that rely on the accurate synthesis of data from multiple sources.

Underreporting practices contribute to metaanalysts overlooking procedural flexibility, leading them to treat substantially different IGT procedures as equivalent (see review of meta-analyses in the introduction).
Clinical studies showed a substantially higher rate of indeterminable procedural details than nonclinical studies (65.63% vs.
Notably, clinical and non-clinical studies were not matched on journal type, research design, or other factors that may influence reporting practices.
Nonetheless, this finding is consistent with broader evidence that important methodological details are frequently absent from reporting in clinical psychological research.

For examplehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?8aqeye key details about intervention delivery were reported in fewer than half of clinical psychology trials (Grant et al., 2013) , and clinical fMRI studies reported a median of only 51% of task-relevant procedural details (Guo et al., 2014). Tackett et al. (2017) have argued that clinical psychology has been slower than other subfields to engage with open science reforms, describing structural barriers which may partly account for these patterns.

(2017)</ref> have argued that clinical psychology has been slower than other subfields to engage with open science reforms, describing structural barriers which may partly account for these patterns.

text.text: Importantly, while guidelines such as CONSORT (Schulz et al., 2010) and JARS (Appelbaum et al., 2018) require sufficient detail to allow replication, they leave considerable latitude for what sufficient detail means in practice for behavioral tasks specifically, which may lead researchers to default to minimal reporting, especially when this is the reporting norm in their field anyway.

text.text: Word limits imposed by journals may compound this further.

The recently introduced PECANS checklist (Costa et al., 2025) was released to address this gap, providing more granular guidance for reporting of procedures in cognitive and neuropsychological research.
text.formatted: The recently introduced PECANS checklist <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Costa et al., 2025)</ref> was released to address this gap, providing more granular guidance for reporting of procedures in cognitive and neuropsychological research.

text.text: We recommend that future IGT studies use PECANS as a reporting guideline (especially sections 25 and 26).
It is the norm, rather than the exception, that the IGT is modified for a study on a range of procedural aspects, either in isolation or combined.

Although these modifications may be pragmatic solutions in specific contextshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?X8PTqQ they also introduce new dynamics to the task that might differ from the original and may influence participant behaviour (Areias et al., 2013) , often to an unknown degree when not validated first (Elson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Although these modifications may be pragmatic solutions in specific contexts, they also introduce new dynamics to the task that might differ from the original and may influence participant behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Areias et al., 2013)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?X8PTqQ">,</ref> often to an unknown degree when not validated first <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Elson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Further, IGT papers often do not offer a rationale for why a modification was necessary, and simply state them as such.
Consequently, whether results from modified IGTs can be compared to studies employing the original IGT, the clinical IGT, or any other variants is often unclear.
This may contribute to the formation of erroneous beliefs regarding the constructs a given IGT variant is measuring, referred to as jingle fallacy.
A jingle fallacy (Thorndike, 1904) occurs when different constructs are mistakenly treated as the same because they share the same label.
text.formatted: A jingle fallacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Thorndike, 1904)</ref> occurs when different constructs are mistakenly treated as the same because they share the same label.

text.text: This situation may arise when various unvalidated IGT variants and scoring methods are assumed to measure the same underlying construct.
Although a nominally standardised IGT for clinical use and research exists (Becharahttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?QdW4p7 2007 (Bechara, , 2016)) , it was only employed in a fraction of cases.

text.text: One possible explanation could be the commercial licensing of the software and the norm data.
For instance, the official IGT Digital Kit costs 268 USD, which includes the e-manual and 25 on-screen administrations and reports.
Subsequent uses incur additional costs of 4.20 USD per administration and 3.00 USD per report as of January 9, 2026 (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?4wZV6q.
text.formatted: Subsequent uses incur additional costs of 4.20 USD per administration and 3.00 USD per report as of January 9, 2026 (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?4wZV6q">PAR,  Inc., n.d.)</ref>.

text.text: These costs can accumulate in particular in larger studies with limited budgets, potentially hindering the wide-spread use of the clinical IGT.
The accessibility of standardized open-source software and an open data set with norm data may provide an effective solution to this issue.
A key finding was the high degree of scoring flexibility with 244 distinct scores of which only 67 were used more than once.
Although a small established subset of scores is used frequently, idiosyncratic, inconsistent, or poorly defined scoring methods vary substantially between studies.
These scores often reflect novel attempts to capture specific behaviors or outcomes, but have not been validated or replicated in other studies.
Their psychometric properties are largely unknown at the time of their first use, and they usually remain unexplored.
The multiverse analysis demonstrates that correlations among scoring methods can range from strong convergence through near-zero association to strong divergence and everything in between.

Nor do these relationships among scoring methods reduce to a smaller underlying structure: hierarchical clustering showed gradients in a continuously structured metric space rather than discrete partitions.

Within-cluster correlations are too modest for any single score to substitute for the others in its cluster, and between-cluster correlations remain high enough that the clusters do not constitute well-separated dimensions.
The fragmentation documented here cannot be remedied by collapsing scores onto a handful of representative metrics.
It becomes difficult to distinguish this situation from one in which no single construct is being measured consistently, while still being interpreted as "IGT scores".

We believe there is a strong risk of a large-scale jingle fallacy in the IGT literature, though without systematic validation of IGT scores, there is little evidence in favor or against this hypothesis.
The broad spectrum of scoring methods adopted in IGT studies which do not necessarily correlate gives rise to concerns about the potential for exploiting researcher degrees of freedom and phacking.
These scoring practices allow researchers to easily select scoring approaches after the fact that yield the most favorable outcomes.
Results that are the product of opportunistic selection of scoring methods have a higher probability of being false positives and are unlikely to replicate in a new sample (Simmons et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Results that are the product of opportunistic selection of scoring methods have a higher probability of being false positives and are unlikely to replicate in a new sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Simmons et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This raises concerns regarding the credibility of literature heavily using the IGT, as it becomes increasingly challenging to distinguish between robust findings and those that are the consequence of exploiting researcher degrees of freedom.
This is particularly worrying when IGT-based findings are put into practice, e.g. in clinical populations.
What can researchers do to defend their scoring choice?
Preregistration constrains analytical flexibility, but a poorly defined or psychometrically inadequate score can be locked in as easily as a defensible one.

We suggest evaluating candidate scoring methods against four substantive criteria: 1) conceptual alignment with the construct of interest, 2) unambiguous computability from a clearly described procedure, 3) compatibility with the procedural details actually used (e.g., trial count and gain-loss schedule), and 4) prior use in the literature with a clear specification.

Reliability operates within these criteria rather than as a standalone gate, since reliability estimates exist for only a handful of scores and the available estimates are modest (r .27 to .37 for the net score across ≈ studies, see Buelow & Barnhart, 2018b; Schmitz et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Reliability operates within these criteria rather than as a standalone gate, since reliability estimates exist for only a handful of scores and the available estimates are modest (r .27 to .37 for the net score across ≈ studies, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Buelow & Barnhart, 2018b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Schmitz et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Xu et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Applied to the scores documented in this review, the net score across all 100 trials and the five-block learning index are arguably the most defensible defaults for the 100trial task since both are modal in the literature (criterion 4), and both can be computed unambiguously from data collected with the dominant ABCD variant (criteria 2 and 3), though only if they are appropriate for the research question (criterion 1).
Despite its nominal standardisation, we are less inclined to recommend the clinical IGT as a research default.
The professional manual reports no reliability data, and its non-stationary gain-loss schedule limits comparability with the much larger body of work using the contingencies from the original task.

The T-score conversions distributed with the clinical IGT cannot be substituted by manual post-calculation from data collected with another variant, because the norms are calibrated to that procedure.
Further constraints should be considered when conducting analyses on secondary IGT data to avoid suspicions of post-hoc selection.

For example, where the dataset is large enough, splitting the data to create a hold-out sample until the analysis plan is fixed could produce a confirmatory test that is structurally similar to a preregistration prior to data collection, assuming no leakage between the analyses (Baldwin et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For example, where the dataset is large enough, splitting the data to create a hold-out sample until the analysis plan is fixed could produce a confirmatory test that is structurally similar to a preregistration prior to data collection, assuming no leakage between the analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baldwin et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The IGT is unlikely to be unique in the degree of methodological flexibility we document here.

Many widely used behavioral paradigms in psychology similarly exist as families of loosely related procedures that share a common name but may differ in implementation details, stimulus parameters, and scoring conventions.
While this heterogeneity is often acknowledged informally, it has only occasionally been systematically quantified.
For example, Jones et al. (2021) identified about 9,000 possible analytical strategies for the addiction Stroop task.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Jones et al. (2021)</ref> identified about 9,000 possible analytical strategies for the addiction Stroop task.

text.text: Meta-method reviews (Elson, 2019) offer a systematic approach for quantifying this flexibility and its consequences, and we would encourage its application to other commonly used paradigms across the behavioral sciences.
text.formatted: Meta-method reviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Elson, 2019)</ref> offer a systematic approach for quantifying this flexibility and its consequences, and we would encourage its application to other commonly used paradigms across the behavioral sciences.

text.text: However, the findings suggest that whenever a paradigm permits substantial researcher degrees of freedom in both administration and scoring, the resulting literature may be far less cumulative than it appears.
Such efforts would help the field identify where the appearance of methodological consensus masks substantial hidden heterogeneity.
This is a prerequisite for determining whether and how findings from these paradigms can meaningfully be compared, aggregated, or replicated.

Critically, this also concerns research synthesis: as our review of 15 meta-analyses demonstrates, procedural heterogeneity in primary studies can go entirely unaccounted for at the metaanalytic level, potentially compromising the conclusions drawn from aggregated evidence.
More broadly, our findings highlight a fundamental tension in psychological measurement between the adaptability that researchers value and the standardization that cumulative science requires.

The multiverse analysis illustrates the potential consequences: two researchers analyzing the same IGT data could arrive at conclusions that converge, diverge, or bear no relation to one another, depending on which of the many available scoring approaches they select.
This points to the value of multiverse analyses as a diagnostic instrument for evaluating the coherence of measurement practices across a field.

When a multiverse of scoring strategies yields a median inter-correlation near zero, this can be understood as evidence that the construct validity of the paradigm's outputs has not been established, and that claims derived from any single, unvalidated scoring approach should be treated with caution.
Our review comes with a number of limitations.

First, our preregistration was light, and we iteratively revised the codebook after the initial preregistration, as a more structured approach to variable coding proved necessary than initially anticipated.
Second, we restricted our sample to 100 peerreviewed publications and consequently, our findings may not be fully reflective of the entire body of IGT literature.

While our use of systematic search and random sampling of studies from the literature ensures the representativeness of our results, as we discuss in the results, it is difficult to estimate the full extent of the flexibility in the population of the full IGT literature.

Third, since it was not feasible to contact all study authors, we accepted the authors' descriptions of their methods in a given publication at face value and did not request more accurate descriptions, data, or analysis scripts.
Because of the high rate of indeterminability in the procedural variables, this approach left many of them unresolved.
The substantial indeterminability limits our understanding of the true variability in IGT procedures across different studies.
Although our review demonstrates that there is considerable procedural flexibility between studies, it needs to be understood as a conservative estimate of its true extent.
It is also worth noting that indeterminable flexibility arguably poses a greater challenge to the interpretation and synthesis of results than determinable degrees of flexibility.

Fourth, while the overall interrater reliability (Cohen's kappa of .70) suggests a substantial degree of agreement between raters, the variability in kappa values across different variables (ranging from .44 to .90) indicates that the reliability of coding depended on the specific procedural detail being assessed.

The interrater reliability was generally high for variables that were less frequently indeterminable and lower for variables with high rates of indeterminability as highlighted by the data: the four variables with the lowest reliability had an average indeterminability rate of 66.75%, compared to an overall average of 50.94% across all variables.
This further emphasizes that the results for the variables with high indeterminability rate should be interpreted with caution.
The main reasons for indeterminability were missing information, vagueness, ambiguities, and inconsistencies in the reporting of specific task procedures.
Here, resolving differences between the two rater's codings proved challenging and required discussion.

As this also highlights a shortcoming in the codebooks for these variables, future metamethod reviews may benefit from more detailed codebook instructions to handle ambiguous and vague methodological descriptions during coding, thereby improving reliability.

We would also recommend for future meta-method reviews to implement a blinded resolution process, whereby a third independent rater reviews any discrepancies in order to minimize the potential for bias.

Fifth, a more ideal approach to multiverse analysis would assess not only the degree to which different ways of scoring IGT data correlated with one another (as our analysis did), but also the degree to which the magnitude of correlations with other tasks varied between these scores (i.e., variation in convergent, discriminant or criterion validity).
Unfortunately, we could not obtain a large and openly available dataset of trial-level IGT data that also included such additional variables.
Future research could assess this through novel data collection.
In summary, our review shows a high prevalence of methodological flexibility in the use of the IGT.

While this is reflective of the diverse research contexts in which the IGT is employed, it comes with substantial challenges for the interpretation, comparability, reproducibility and synthesis of findings.

Given our findings, results from "the IGT", generically described and in the absence of substantive additional information about which specific procedural and scoring choices were employed, are rendered uninterpretable.

Especially concerning is the inconsistent use of a multitude of scoring methods, which are distributed on a spectrum of relationships ranging from strong convergence to near-zero association to strong divergence.
This raises questions about the overall reliability and validity of IGT outcomes and greatly increases the opportunity for p-hacking.

In order for researchers to make meaningful progress in this field, it is essential that they adopt more standardized approaches to IGT procedures and scoring methods in their primary research, and that they ensure transparency and thorough documentation of any modifications.
Such an approach will enhance the robustness and credibility of the IGT as a tool for studying decision-making.
